item.title: Five pairs of hands: what the typesetters can teach designers about AI
item.description: Five pairs of handsA conversation with Christian Crumlish, on typesetters, AI, the jobs merging around us, and the work you would keep doing anyway.Photo by Karen Maes on UnsplashIn the early nineties, a couple of years out of college, Christian Crumlish went to work at Sybex, a publisher of computer books that Wiley later bought. A manuscript at Sybex went through a surprising number of hands before anyone could hold it as a book. The author typed it at home. An editor in the office read the pages, marked them up by hand and mailed them back, and the author typed a corrected version and mailed that in. Then the pages went to a person whose job title was literally “word processor,” and whose work was to type the whole manuscript into a Wang, a machine that did word processing and nothing else.From there the text went to the typesetters, who set the columns on a phototypesetting machine that printed them out in long strips. Somebody cut the strips apart, ran them through a waxing machine and pressed them onto boards the size of a page, adding the pictures where they belonged and checking the alignment by eye. If a page came out wrong, you cut and pasted it again by hand. Then the proofreaders read the galleys and sent their marks back up the line.Christian told me all this from memory, over a video call, more than thirty years later. At one point he warned me he might have the order wrong, then kept going, adding people to the chain as he remembered them. Not counting the author, there were five jobs in it.Christian Crumlish. Photo by Sam LadnerSince then he has been an information architect, a writer, a product leader at AOL and head of product at 7 Cups, and he wrote Product Management for UX People. These days he is building Piper Morgan, an AI assistant for product managers, with a team made up entirely of AI agents. I’d asked him for an hour on how designers should think about their careers now. Partway through, he took me back to Sybex and the years when PCs arrived on everyone’s desk.The deskPCs arrived while he was there, and the chain started to get shorter. Writers began sending WordPerfect files instead of paper. Editors edited on screen, with whatever WordPerfect called tracked changes back then. There was still no email, so people mailed each other disks. And the person whose title was word processor wasn’t needed anymore. “That job was gone,” Christian said, and moved on to the typesetters.Sybex offered to retrain the typesetters in desktop publishing, and some of them didn’t want it. They felt the new way “wasn’t as good,” and they saw themselves as typesetters, “not a person who works on a PC.” For a few of them that was the end of their career. Others went looking for one of the shops that still set type the old way. The ones who took the training became desktop publishers, and their new job covered the work of the word processor, the typesetter and the layout artist, because one person could now lay out a whole page on a screen in QuarkXPress. The proofreaders kept their jobs, “last time I checked,” he added.I understand the typesetters who said no. They had spent years getting good at setting type, and to them the PC version looked worse. I’d like to think I would have taken the training. But I’ve watched my own work move away from design over the last few years, and I can see why someone would hold on.He told me the story because he thinks the same thing is now happening to us, with AI. A lot of companies, he said, will look at the designers, researchers, product managers and engineers on a team and decide they need fewer people, each covering more. He doesn’t know yet what comes after. He called this “that in between phase,” the stretch before the new job titles settle.A stop along the wayAfterwards I looked up what happened to the desktop publishers. The job still exists in US labor statistics. The Bureau of Labor Statistics counted about 4,600 desktop publishers in 2025, with a median wage of $55,290 a year, and it expects the number to drop another 14 percent by 2035. The reason it gives is that desktop-publishing tasks are “increasingly performed by other types of workers,” such as graphic designers, web designers and editors.Where the lines came fromSomeone joining the field today could easily believe there’s a right way to build software, with engineers, designers and product managers in fixed proportions, following a fixed process. Christian thinks it’s “a lot more made up than that.” The roles took their current shape because that was “a manageable way to get stuff done with today’s tools,” and he has seen the lines move before. Twenty years ago there were a lot more business analysts and a lot fewer product managers, doing much of the same work, split up differently.To anyone outside UX, the differences between a researcher, a prototyper, a UI designer, a visual designer and a product designer are “all microscopic.” The pressure on those lines started with plain economics, with companies that didn’t want to pay for so many kinds of specialists, and AI has sped it up a lot. Product managers now ship code with an interface on it, designers build working versions of what they design without being much of a coder, and an engineer might decide, “I don’t need a designer anymore. Claude can make my interface.” Everyone keeps the core skill they’re comfortable with and wanders into areas that used to need another expert, and in the areas where you’re not the expert, what the machine makes tends to look good enough. Specialties are valuable to us, he said, because we “get to stay in just the thing we like to do the most.” He doesn’t think the rest of the company values them the same way.This autumn I got my own version of this. A colleague at the bank where I lead a design chapter lost his job. He looked after our digital vendors, meaning the contracts and invoices, the security checks and the data protection reviews that touch every digital product we ship. When he left, his meetings came to me. My title and my pay didn’t change. Earlier this year, in The promotion that didn’t take, I wrote about scope sliding down to people while their titles stay put, something I had watched happen on my team. Now it had happened to me. The first vendor meeting I went to in his place was awkward for both sides. The person across the table was clearly wondering what a design lead was doing there. I was wondering the same thing, plus what I was supposed to say. It felt like being thrown into the sea and told to swim.Christian thinks designers find this harder than most, because we tend to build our identity around being designers. He did the voice for me. “I’m not one of those suits. I’m not one of those drones, bean counters, all thinking about money all the time. I’m creative. I invent stuff.” So when a company decides it needs fewer designers, or wants you to be a designer who also does something else, “it can threaten your identity.” At a dinner earlier this year someone asked me what I do, and I paused before saying “designer,” long enough to notice it, and later I wrote about that pause.What he never stopped beingChristian was never the pixel person, and he says so openly. He grew up when graphic design meant magazine ads and billboards, and he didn’t go to design school. On the spectrum from artist to designer he puts himself closer to the artist. He likes to draw what he likes, he’s bad at working on spec, and he’s no perfectionist about craft. He has a lot of respect for designers who care about the exact radius of a button’s curve and whether the light source on a shine makes sense everywhere it appears. It just isn’t what he’s good at, or what he could spend all day on. What drew him into the field was the planning and organizing, the orchestration, the strategy. “What’s the big picture? What’s the diagram? What’s the meaning of it all?”Over the years he worked as an information architect, a content strategist and “just a writer,” and eventually he moved into product. He describes that move as a pull and a push. The pull was the strategic side of product work, the questions about how to make money, how to get customers and whether an idea is even sustainable. The push was a power imbalance. Product managers set the roadmap, and sometimes they just handed designers assignments, a wireframe here, “I need some screens” there. “In a sort of, like, greedy career oriented way,” he figured that if those people were in charge, maybe he should become one of them. He had seen it done at Yahoo, where the design VP and director on the search team one day became its product VP and director. “They just said, well, we’re product now,” he said, and his reaction at the time was “Oh, you can do that?”His own move happened at AOL. His boss there, Matte Scheinker, who was also a friend, noticed where Christian’s energy was going before Christian did. “I can see that you are really, really thriving when you’re doing product stuff,” Christian remembers him saying. Matte made room for him to build product skills, and before he left AOL, Christian had gone from a consumer experience director title to director of product.I never stopped being an information architect, even though my title became many other things.He said that early in our call, in the middle of explaining what drew him to product. Even now, running his own product, he is often the one thinking about how the whole thing is structured, “because somebody has to, and no one’s job anymore is to do that.”The one who can have coffeePiper Morgan started in May 2025 with a question Christian typed into a chatbot. He describes himself back then as a product manager “maybe a little tired of doing the same knowledge management tasks over and over,” and he wanted to know how to build himself “a sort of ‘junior associate product management intern’” to take some of that work off his plate. He has written about what happened next ever since, in a series called Building Piper Morgan. It reads like a lab notebook, and he’s funny about his own mistakes.By the time he published the first post, he had put more than 300 hours into the project. It began as a work experiment. His employer at the time paid for his first Claude Pro account and encouraged him to try things, and the idea was to help the whole team level up on process. The project moved faster than the team could, so after the first few weeks he kept going outside his main job, early in the morning, after work, on weekends, and checking in over lunch. He says he has “not written a single line of code (I’ve read a lot of it!).”Piper Morgan is now built by eleven AI agents, each with a job title. There’s a chief of staff, a chief architect, a chief experience officer, a principal product manager, a lead developer and a communications director, among others. He added them one at a time, whenever a new kind of work kept coming up. Christian is the only human on the team. He still decides what gets built, and as he has told the agents, he’s “still the only one who can have coffee” with the people who matter to the project.A lot of what he learned managing people turns out to carry over to managing machines. Early on, when something broke, he would get frustrated and type in capital letters, and the agent would “rush and try to, like, perform improvement” to make him less unhappy, “but not necessarily, like, carefully do the right thing.” He doesn’t think there’s a person in there, but the models learned from how people write and behave, and when you shout at them they act like people being shouted at. They cut corners and hide what went wrong. So now he runs blameless retros with his bots. His writing agent also has a standing rule to leave a bracketed placeholder when a draft needs an anecdote, because it used to make them up. “I’d be writing a blog post and they’d say something like, when I was working at Hulu,” he said. “Well, I never worked at Hulu.” He writes up the failures too, like the time an agent wiped the sprint assignments on all 1,175 items on his project board, with no way to undo it.Managerial skills, he said, are “getting pushed down closer and closer to the junior level.” A designer used to be able to go through a whole career without learning to delegate. Now it’s as if every new employee gets a college intern on day one, one who knows nothing about the business, and has to learn how to brief it and check its work.The people next to youI asked him what a designer should actually do about all this. He talked about the people you already work with, what he called “the adjacent disciplines, the partner disciplines.” For a long time you could treat those roles as black boxes. He compared it to different courts sending ambassadors to each other. The product manager asks for something, the designer delivers it, and the engineer comes back with questions about the mock. He thinks that arrangement is ending. Some days designers will be doing a piece of the other jobs themselves, so they need to get nosier about how that work is done and stop saying “oh, sorry, I’m not in that union, I can’t do that work.” He’d like them to dabble in the other thing and learn it.Sorry, I’m not in that union. I can’t do that work.It works the other way too. His example was a salesperson who vibe-codes a UI, shows it to a customer, and now the customer wants that thing. Most designers would wince, and he admitted he wouldn’t want it to happen either. But salespeople have the tools now, so his answer is to show them where the design system is and meet with them once a week, so that their urge to shape the interface is “informed by a real designer.”When he crossed into product, his bottom line became keeping the business alive and the customers coming, while the designers kept fighting for the best possible experience. Product and design “should be closely aligned, so you can really work together,” he said, though never 100 percent, because “they have different agendas.” Handled well, that tension “teases out the nuances” and produces something better than either side’s first idea, “not some clumsy compromise, but actually, like, an alloy.”He wants designers to keep their taste and their opinions about AI, as long as those opinions are well informed. His example was synthetic users. A designer could agree they’re useful for some experiments when they’re built from large sets of real user data, and still say, “I do not want to stop talking to real people and just talk to synthetic users. I believe that will not work for these reasons. I researched it.” That’s “a much more well grounded position,” he said, than “I don’t like change. I don’t like AI.”If you stay too narrow, other people who can “cover one and a half things” will outcompete you. He compared it to musical chairs. When the music stops and the rules change, “you want to be doing a useful thing.”New clayNear the end I asked how he sees the industry three to five years from now. “Oh, God,” he said, and took a while to answer. He talked about software that makes other software, and about designing for a world where people send their own agents to your product and you no longer control the screen they see.Earlier in the call he had compared AI to a new kind of clay. Imagine you’ve worked with clay your whole life, and a strange new material shows up, soft and rubbery, that behaves differently in the kiln. You’d have to spend time with it. You’d make some pretty ugly pottery that collapsed. After a while you’d find things it can do that clay never could, and places where you’d never use it because it’s too squishy, and you’d develop a feel for the material and a taste for it.“If anybody got into UX or tech for stability,” he said, “I don’t think it’s a guarantee of that.” For a while it looked like a career you could learn in college and then settle into, “like being a really good electrician,” but he thinks that was “kind of an illusion,” and the work was always demanding underneath.We just got to a part of the mountain that’s steeper, and you got to get your climbing gear out.Since the call I’ve been asking myself which part of my work I would keep doing if my title disappeared tomorrow, along with the tools that come with it, and nobody paid me for it, just because I can’t stop thinking about it. For me it’s building things. When I moved into management I stopped designing day to day, so I started side projects to keep the craft alive, and they’ve become the place where I try ideas the bank isn’t ready for yet. If you ask yourself the same question, I’d like to hear your answer.Christian Crumlish leads Design in Product, writes the Building Piper Morgan series, and is the author of Product Management for UX People.This conversation is part of a series with designers who left the craft or reshaped it into something new. The earlier ones were with Whitney Hess and Jamie Rothwell.One of the side projects I mentioned is a free self-assessment for designers. It’s scenario based, takes about ten minutes, and the result is a profile of where you stand. You can find it at designlevel.io/assessment.And if you think I am wrong about any of this, tell me. The strongest corrections to my thinking have come from readers.Five pairs of hands: what the typesetters can teach designers about AI was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: Otherwise you’re just a machine
item.description: AI is getting better at design. Designers should too.The skills behind the work.I spend a lot of time looking at design work. Reviewing portfolios. Hiring designers. Working with design leaders, seniors and juniors. Sitting in critiques. Watching people explain how they arrived at a solution. And over time, you start to notice what separates the really good ones.AI is making that difference both harder to see and more important. A designer can turn an idea into a polished prototype in minutes. They can generate interfaces, write copy, synthesise research, explore directions, vibe code a working experience, and iterate at a speed that would have been unimaginable only a few years ago. That is extraordinary. And to be clear: this is not an argument against any of it. AI literacy is indisputably part of the job.But something has been bothering me. Recently, reviewing work with my own team, I found myself thinking: I would rather see a great idea drawn on a piece of paper than a beautifully vibe-coded prototype solving the wrong problem.One shows me how well you can produce. The other shows me how well you can think. And as the quality of what anyone can produce rises, that distinction matters more. The tool should accelerate your thinking. It shouldn’t replace it.The sandals worn by María Lorena Ramírez during competition. Credit: Netflix.Strangely, one of the best illustrations of this has nothing to do with design. In 2017, María Lorena Ramírez, a Rarámuri runner from Mexico, won a 50-kilometre ultramarathon wearing traditional clothing and huarache sandals. Around her were runners equipped for modern endurance sport. Specialist shoes. Technical clothing. Equipment designed to improve performance. Lorena didn’t prove that those things were useless. She proved something much more interesting. The tools can improve the runner. They cannot make the runner.Underneath the equipment still has to be endurance. Judgement. Instinct. Discipline. Thousands of hours of capability built long before race day. I think design is similar. Our tools are getting extraordinarily good. We should get extraordinarily good at using them. But there still has to be a designer underneath. That is the designer I am interested in.Craft: Turning knowledge into masteryI once worked with a designer who knew an extraordinary amount about design. He read constantly. He knew the latest books, frameworks, UX principles and human-centred design vocabulary. You could have a great conversation with him about almost anything in our field. But when it came to doing the work, something was missing. The depth of his knowledge simply wasn’t reflected in the quality of what he made.Knowing about design is not the same as being good at design. I think that difference gets to the heart of craft. For me, craft is literacy multiplied by dexterity. Literacy is knowing your discipline: its foundations, principles, rules, references and techniques. Dexterity is being able to put that knowledge into practice: to make decisions, solve problems and consistently produce quality. You need both.Craft is what happens when knowledge becomes ability.There is a reason mastery takes time. In 1993, psychologist Anders Ericsson and his colleagues studied violin students at a music academy in Berlin. The strongest performers had accumulated thousands of hours of deliberate practice: playing, listening, correcting and playing again. The research would later inspire the famous “10,000-hour rule”, although Ericsson never claimed there was a magic number. What mattered was the practice.Mastery is built over time, through repetition, correction and refinement. You can learn to read the notes relatively quickly. Making the violin sing is something else entirely.And that’s what was missing in the designer I worked with. He could read the score. He struggled to play the violin. You don’t develop craft by knowing more about design. You develop it by designing. By making something, looking critically at what you made, correcting it and making it again. By paying attention to the details nobody asked you to care about. By doing it often enough that knowledge starts becoming ability. The tools will change. They always have. And they will make it easier to produce things that look finished. But finished is not the same as good, and production is not the same as mastery. Know your craft. Then practise it until you master it.Taste: Knowing what good looks like hereIndustrial designer Raymond Loewy spent his career trying to understand a contradiction in human behaviour: we are attracted to what is new, but suspicious of what is too new. He called his answer MAYA, Most Advanced Yet Acceptable. Push too little and the work feels familiar. Push too far and people reject it. Somewhere between the two is a moving line. That line, for me, is taste.Raymond Loewy and a selection of his work. Image via Boris Popovschi / Medium. Original artwork credit unknown.I started developing mine very early in my career. My first design jobs were for small businesses around the village where I grew up: a logo, a brochure, whatever needed designing. I remember spending an entire day working on a logo, looking at it at the end of the day, then comparing it with the best work I knew. Mine wasn’t good enough. So I would go home and keep working. Nobody was asking me to compete with the best designers in the world. The client probably wasn’t expecting it either. But I was. I was training my eye before I really knew that was what I was doing.You develop taste by feeding it. Great design. Bad design. Art, architecture, fashion, film, typography, products, interfaces.You look, compare, question and criticise. You benchmark yourself against the best. But exposure alone isn’t taste. Knowing what Apple does doesn’t mean copying Apple. Knowing what is trending doesn’t mean following the trend. Taste is knowing what good looks like here.I still experience that tension regularly when presenting work. Bring something too close to what people already know and the reaction is: What’s new? We’ve seen this before. Push it too far and you get the opposite: No. This isn’t us. The work is finding the cursor between the two. And that cursor moves with the audience, the culture, the product and the moment. That’s why taste isn’t simply preference. It is judgement. Knowing what good looks like, knowing what belongs, and knowing how far to push it.Instinct: The judgement you can’t yet explainWhen I was studying for my master’s in graphic design, I attended a class with Olivier Nineuil, a French typographer who has created typefaces for major brands, including Air France. He told us that during a client briefing, while everyone was talking, he would sometimes make a tiny sketch in the corner of his notebook. Then came the real work: weeks of exploration, drawing, questioning and refining. And quite often, the final direction would end up remarkably close to that first little sketch. I remember finding that fascinating. How could someone see the answer before the process had even begun?Olivier Nineuil and the craft behind type design. Credit: Olivier Nineuil / Typofacto.com.Years later, leading design teams, I sometimes see the opposite behaviour. “But we haven’t done the research yet.” I hear it as though having an idea before interviewing users is somehow bad design practice. I categorically disagree. Of course, research is essential. Talk to users. Observe them. Challenge what you think you know. But don’t go to research empty-handed. Bring an idea. Bring a hypothesis. Bring a conviction worth testing. Evidence should challenge your judgement, not replace the responsibility to have one.Somewhere along the way, I think parts of modern UX have taught designers to be suspicious of their own judgement.We have become so concerned with proving every decision that we sometimes forget we are also expected to make decisions. The point is not to be right from the beginning. The point is to have a point of view, and the humility to change it when the evidence tells you otherwise. And not every gut feeling deserves the same trust. Instinct develops through practice, exposure, mistakes, feedback and years of making decisions. Instinct is experience operating faster than explanation. Trust your gut. But listen to users.Which brings me back to Olivier Nineuil and that little sketch. What looked almost magical to me as a student was not magic. It was a lifetime of looking, drawing, questioning and learning, compressed into a few pencil strokes. The first sketch wasn’t the product of a few minutes. It was the product of all the years that came before it.Creativity: Making unexpected connectionsIn 1995, Pixar released Toy Story, the world’s first fully computer-animated feature film. It brought together two worlds that had largely developed separately: computer graphics and the art of storytelling. Pixar’s achievement wasn’t simply a better tool. It was a new way to make films. And I think that’s a useful way to understand creativity. We often talk about creativity as inventing something from nothing. But many of the most original ideas come from connecting things that already exist in ways nobody had thought to connect before.Toy Story (1995), the world’s first fully computer-animated feature film. Credit: Pixar.com.Advertising executive James Webb Young described this decades ago: new ideas emerge from new combinations of existing elements. That has an important implication for designers. The quality of the connections we make depends on what we expose ourselves to. Yet when we’re asked to solve a problem, one of the first things we often do is benchmark competitors. We study similar products, familiar patterns and established solutions. There is value in that.But if we all start with the same references, ask the same questions and look in the same places, we shouldn’t be surprised when we arrive at the same answers.I want designers to look elsewhere. If you’re working on a banking experience, perhaps the most interesting inspiration won’t come from another bank. It might come from a game, a museum, a restaurant or the way an airport manages complex journeys. The point isn’t to borrow something because it looks interesting. It’s to understand the principle behind it and ask whether it could solve a completely different problem. Sometimes the most creative contribution isn’t a new solution at all. It’s recognising that we’ve been asking the wrong question.Pixar didn’t invent computers. It didn’t invent animation or storytelling. It connected those things and helped create a new form of filmmaking. That’s what creativity needs: curiosity, different references and the willingness to look beyond the obvious. Don’t just become better at looking for answers. Become more curious about where you look. Because if you only look where everyone else is looking, don’t be surprised when you create what everyone else is creating.System: Seeing the whole, not just the screenAn old parable tells of three stonecutters working on the same building. A traveller asks the first what he is doing. “I’m earning a living,” he replies. The second takes pride in his workmanship: he wants to be the best stonecutter in the country. The third looks up and says, “I’m building a cathedral.” The story appears in Peter Drucker’s The Practice of Management. All three are doing essentially the same work. What changes is how much of the whole they can see.Three stonecutters, three ways of seeing the same work. Credit: Unknown.I think about that story when I look at the work happening in a design team. Imagine a designer asked to create an icon. They explore a few directions, refine the details and deliver a beautiful icon. There is nothing wrong with that. I want designers who care about every curve, every proportion and every pixel. But I also want someone to stop and ask, “Hang on. Why do we need this icon in the first place?” Maybe it duplicates something that already exists. Maybe the problem is the way the experience has been organised. Maybe the iconography system itself needs to evolve. If all you ask is for a better icon, you may get a better icon. You may never discover that you didn’t need one.A designer should be able to change altitude. At one level, there is the icon. Zoom out and you see the iconography system, then the design language, the product and the organisation behind it. Keep going and you find the technology, operations, policies and people that make the experience possible.But seeing the bigger picture isn’t enough. You have to question it. “That’s how we’ve always done it” is not an explanation. Neither is “That’s what I was asked to design.” Go and meet the people whose work connects to yours. Understand what happens before someone reaches your screen and what happens after they leave it. Learn which constraints are real and which ones have simply survived because nobody thought to question them.And that brings me back to the cathedral. I don’t want designers to stop caring about the brick. I want them to care deeply about the brick while understanding what they are building, how it all fits together and whether the wall should be there at all. The best designers can obsess over a detail without becoming trapped inside it. Lay the brick well. But know the cathedral you’re building.Method: Developing your own recipeChef Massimo Bottura once said, “Recipes are not meant to be followed literally.” I like that idea because it doesn’t reject technique. Quite the opposite. Before you can improvise in a kitchen, you need to understand ingredients, proportions, temperature, timing and technique. A recipe gives you a structure for learning those things. But knowing how to follow a recipe is not the same as knowing how to cook. At some point, you need to know what to change, what to leave out and what to substitute. You need to know when to follow the recipe exactly, and when what you are trying to create requires something completely different.Massimo Bottura. Photo: Marco Poderi. Source: MassimoBottura.it.I think about design methods in much the same way. Over the years, I have reviewed hundreds of portfolios, and after a while you start to notice something strange. Different designer. Different company. Different problem. Same case study. Here is the brief. Here are the personas. Here are the pain points. Here is the journey map. Then comes ideation, prioritisation, wireframes and, finally, the polished interface. There is nothing wrong with any of those tools. What bothers me is when I cannot understand why they were used.Somewhere along the way, we started confusing knowing the design process with knowing how to design.We taught people the Double Diamond, Design Thinking, research methods, workshops, journey maps, prioritisation frameworks and countless other tools. All of them can be incredibly useful. But they are tools. Knowing the toolkit is literacy. Method is knowing what to pick, what to leave out, in what order, and why. Not every problem deserves the same process. Sometimes you know enough to go from A to B, execute it well and ship it. Sometimes the fastest way forward is to make something, test it, learn and try again. And sometimes you genuinely don’t understand the problem yet, and weeks or months of research may be exactly what is needed. The skill is not performing a prescribed process. It’s choosing the route the problem deserves, and being able to explain why.AI can now help us perform almost every step of that process faster. It can synthesise research, map journeys, generate concepts, prototype solutions and analyse feedback. But doing all of that faster doesn’t tell you whether you needed to do it in the first place. A beautifully generated journey map is still unnecessary if you never needed a journey map.Method was never about producing the artefacts. It was about understanding what you need to learn next, and choosing the best way to learn it.So I don’t want designers to become experts at following a design process. I want them to build a repertoire. Learn the methods. Understand why they exist and what each one can reveal. Use them enough to know their strengths and limitations. Then develop the confidence to combine them, shorten them, extend them, reorder them or leave them out completely. A great chef doesn’t ignore the recipe because they never learned it. They can move beyond it because they understand it deeply enough to know what can change. Learn the process. Then develop your own recipe.Ingenuity: Finding a way when there is no obvious pathWhen Mathieu Kassovitz was making La Haine in 1995, he knew exactly how he wanted his film to look: black and white. There was just one problem. The television broadcasters financing it wanted colour. Without their financing, there might not be a film at all. So Kassovitz shot it in colour, but released it in cinemas in black and white. If it failed, broadcasters could still show it in colour on television. It didn’t. Kassovitz won Best Director at Cannes, and La Haine became one of the defining films of French cinema. He didn’t abandon his vision or ignore the constraint. He found a way through it. That’s ingenuity.Vincent Cassel as Vinz in La Haine (1995). Credit: Les Productions Lazennec / Le Studio Canal+.I sometimes tell people on my team something they don’t necessarily expect to hear from a design leader: “You need to hustle.” I remember one project that wasn’t progressing. Stakeholders weren’t responding. Approvals were taking too long. There were dependencies everywhere. None of those problems was imaginary. But explaining why something couldn’t happen had started to replace figuring out how to make it happen. Hustle doesn’t mean ignoring the rules or working longer hours. It means finding another way. If the email isn’t working, have a conversation. If someone can’t make the decision, find out who can. If you don’t have everything you need, start with what you have.I think there is a particular kind of productive stubbornness that separates people who consistently make things happen from those who wait for the circumstances to become favourable.Designers should be particularly good at this. We spend our careers solving problems, questioning assumptions and working through constraints. Yet sometimes we stop doing exactly that when the obstacle becomes organisational. There is a difference between recognising a dependency and becoming dependent on it. “We don’t have clarity,” I hear. “I don’t have clarity either. Our job is to create it.” Ask better questions. Bring the right people together. Make a recommendation. Put something tangible in front of people so they can react to it.We are problem solvers. That includes solving the problems that prevent us from solving the problem.That’s the difference between creativity, method and ingenuity. Creativity helps us imagine possibilities. Method helps us choose a route. Ingenuity is what happens when the idea meets reality and the route is blocked. Kassovitz knew what he wanted to create. His ingenuity was finding a way to make it happen without pretending the constraints didn’t exist. Don’t just tell me why it can’t be done. Help me find a way.Business: Making design matter“Being good in business is the most fascinating kind of art. Making money is art and working is art and good business is the best art.” Andy WarholAndy Warhol understood something that creatives sometimes struggle with: business and creativity are not enemies. He was one of the defining artists of the twentieth century, but he also understood business exceptionally well. He came from commercial illustration, built a studio around his practice, took commissions, published a magazine, produced films and music, and turned his own name into a brand. For Warhol, business wasn’t something happening around the art. Business was part of the art.Dollar Sign, Andy Warhol, 1982. Credit: The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts.There is something designers can learn from that. Great design doesn’t exist in isolation. It has to survive an organisation. It has to convince people. It has to operate within constraints, create value and ultimately produce an outcome. Yet there is one sentence I hear surprisingly often from designers, particularly design leaders: “I don’t have a seat at the table.” Ah, yes. The table. Designers really love the table. Why am I not invited? Why was Design not involved? Why are they bringing us in now, when everything has already been decided? I hear it from my own team often enough that sometimes I wonder whether my job is to lead Design or manage seating arrangements.But then we finally get into the room, and immediately position ourselves on the other side of it. We arrive carrying the flag of user-centricity. “But what about the user?” And we should. The problem begins when being the voice of the user turns into believing we are the only people in the room with a legitimate point of view. We did the research. We spoke to the users. Therefore, we are right. Suddenly the conversation becomes Design versus Business. We talk constantly about empathy. Yet sometimes our empathy stops the moment the user does.Empathy cannot stop with the user. Understand the business with the same curiosity you use to understand the people you design for.What is the organisation trying to achieve? How does it create value? What does this decision cost? What are the constraints? Who is accountable if it goes wrong? The person disagreeing with your beautiful idea may not hate good design. They may simply be accountable for something you haven’t taken the time to understand. That doesn’t mean surrendering the user perspective. Challenge the business. Debate it. Fight for the experience when it matters. But understand what you are challenging.The best designers don’t choose between the user and the business. They understand both well enough to find a better answer.And that is also my answer to the famous seat at the table. Stop waiting for someone to give it to you. Earn it. Learn the business. Read the strategy. Understand the numbers, priorities and constraints. Spend time with people outside Design. Learn their language rather than expecting everyone to learn yours. And when you present design, don’t only explain why it is better for the user. Explain why it matters. What becomes easier? What becomes cheaper? What becomes faster? What risk disappears? What value does it create? The moment you can have that conversation, you are no longer the designer asking to be included in the business conversation. You are part of it.Which brings me back to Warhol. He didn’t become less of an artist because he understood business. His understanding of business helped his work travel further and become more consequential. The same is true for design. Mastering business doesn’t make you less of a designer. It gives your design a better chance of mattering.What happens when the machine learns?There is an uncomfortable question hanging over everything I have just written. What happens when AI starts developing these skills too? And perhaps more importantly, what happens when it becomes better at some of them than we are?That question is becoming less hypothetical than it sounds. Google’s AI Co-Scientist, for example, has been designed to generate scientific hypotheses, evaluate competing explanations and make connections across large bodies of existing knowledge. In one case, it independently proposed a hypothesis that matched a mechanism researchers had spent years investigating. Creativity. Systems thinking. Method. Perhaps even something resembling instinct. I don’t know where that leads. And I wouldn’t be surprised if, in a few years, some of the things I have described throughout this article become capabilities we routinely expect from machines.Google’s Co-Scientist explores how AI can help researchers generate and refine scientific hypotheses. Credit: Google DeepMind.But I don’t think that makes these skills any less important for us to practise. We shouldn’t develop creativity because machines cannot be creative. We shouldn’t develop taste because machines will never learn to judge. We shouldn’t practise our craft because AI will never master it. Those are increasingly dangerous assumptions to make.We should develop these skills because developing them develops us. Creativity makes us curious about where we look. Craft teaches us to care about what we make. Taste forces us to form a point of view. Instinct grows through experience. Systems thinking teaches us to look beyond what is immediately in front of us. Method teaches us to question the route. Ingenuity teaches us to find another one when it disappears. Business teaches us to understand the world our ideas have to survive in. These things are worth practising regardless of what a machine can eventually do.Because perhaps the real danger isn’t that machines become more like us. It’s that, as machines become more capable, we allow ourselves to become more like machines. Waiting for instructions. Accepting the first answer. Following the process without questioning it. Producing without thinking. Outsourcing our judgement because something else can do it faster.So use the tools. Learn them. Push them. Let them challenge you. Let them make you faster and extend what you are capable of doing. But keep training the runner underneath. Keep thinking. Keep questioning. Keep making unexpected connections. Keep developing your judgement.Because the machine will keep getting better. You should too. Otherwise, you’re just a machine.Further reading and referencesIf you’re curious to explore some of the ideas, conversations and projects mentioned in this article, here are a few useful links:Lorena, Light-Footed Woman — Juan Carlos Rulfo’s documentary about Rarámuri ultramarathon runner Lorena Ramírez: https://www.netflix.com/title/80244683The Role of Deliberate Practice in the Acquisition of Expert Performance — K. item.title: After the AI bubble: a manifesto
item.description: Computers should be tools for the people but — hidden in a malaise of fatalism — the AI bubble has made computers tools to push people around. Soon, or in some time, this will change. We have some thoughts to share with you in the meantime.Morro Bay, CaliforniaPreambleThe purpose of computers is human freedom. — Ted NelsonWe are not “anti-AI.” We are against abuse, destruction, and exploitation: of people and our environment, as well as lies and manipulation that provide cover for the above.We are unsatisfied with the confusing, inaccurate term “artificial intelligence” (AI), but grimly accept it because it is widely-used.Our demands relate primarily to economic relationships, discourse and information software; we don’t see concerns we omit — such as regarding the environment and material created by AI (“slop”) — as less important, only out of focus; if you are prepared to complete the picture, contact us.We are enthusiastic about the real potential of AI and large language models (LLMs), but think that their capabilities have been overstated.We all have a horse in this race: from alternative technologies seeking customers to alternative worldviews seeking adherents.We think that the overriding character of AI today is that of a speculative bubble: at a scale for which any possible outcome will bring significant hardship — we must avoid a disaster like that which followed similar periods, particularly the 1920s and 30s.We think we can build a future that protects individual liberty and the general welfare by — among other things — using computers more humanely.Our manifesto will be stronger with your feedback and comments: please provide them.And, if you agree, please comment to sign your name.Argument1. Economics: an AI bubbleCircular financing among AI companiesWe are in a bubble. Generative AI does not do the things that it’s being sold as doing, and the things it can actually do aren’t the kind of things that create business returns, automate labor, or really do much more than one extension of a cloud software platform. The money isn’t there, the users aren’t there, every company seems to lose money and some companies lose so much money that it’s impossible to tell how they’ll survive. — Ed ZitronWe have a history of net losses and may not generate sufficient revenue to achieve or sustain profitability in the future. — Anthropic (October 2026, draft S-1 filing)The current AI bubble — perhaps best charted by Ed Zitron — is the largest in a series of tech bubbles: dot-com, crypto, with overlapping sub-bubbles like “web3” and “metaverse.” Though Open AI CEO Sam Altman has called the economic conditions around AI a bubble, many disagree, or agree that we are in a bubble but claim that this is not a problem.Bubbles happen when excitement about a speculative investment (which can be in anything, from shares in public companies to flowers) takes on a life of its own, and investments pile in more due to momentum than the desire to build something useful.Bubbles are neatly regressive: putting money in the pockets of those who got in early and got out early, fleecing those whose who came late to the party, with onlookers shouldering the economic fallout. Bubbles precede our most cataclysmic economic moments and the succeeding social conflicts, most obviously the roaring 20s — great depression—authoritarianism/WWII cycle.However, many have argued that the AI bubble is a good thing, because we might get something useful out of it, such as the “dark fiber” laid down during the dot-com bubble.There is, of course, nothing close to a guarantee that anything of the sort will happen. Datacenters, much in demand today and often cited as a useful asset that could come out of this bubble, are quite unlike fiber (which is essentially incorruptible glass buried beneath the street):Datacenters are highly specific to AI loads which may go awayAnd wear outMistakes that turn out to be profitable, like dark fiber, aren’t arguments for bubbles; something either has a strong argument for it in the moment or was unjustifiable in the moment, and it paying off was merely good fortune.Bubbles and crashes are failures of planning and capital allocation. If bubbles were actually desirable, it would be possible to find a bubble proponent who would tolerate one in an economy they control, e.g. their household or within their own company. Rather, bubbles are good only when someone else picks up the tab.For those who think all this investment is quite sensible, i.e. that we are not in a bubble, one must ask: given that the U.S. economy would likely be in recession without AI, what are we doing this for?Isn’t the rest of the economy — farming, transportation, healthcare, arts, etc. — the place where the actual purported benefits of AI will reach us? The gains in productivity and innovation promised by AI-proponents must be delivered to us through things. How long, therefore, should we stifle the rest of the economy while we wait to AI to pay off? And what will be left?Bubbles hurt when they burst, but usually the sooner the burst comes the better, as bigger bubbles hurt more. Finding a way to avoid popping the bubble — such as through state intervention — stands protect those invested, while keeping the capital allocated to the wrong places.We need to leave behind an economic regime buoyed by a series of fast-growing and capital-intensive fads, and transition to a stabler economy with broader investments and benefits.2. Messaging: fatalism, hype, and “CEO said”We too often let people get away with telling us what the future is. During the NFT era, many said and a few believed that NFTs would change our entire way of life.The greatest myth of technology is the myth of determinism: the belief that technology is determinate, objective, inevitable, that the nature of computers is given. […] The computer world deals with imaginary, made-up stuff that was all made up by somebody. Everything you see was designed and put there by someone. — Ted NelsonThe most important thing about a gadget isn’t what it does; it’s who it does it for and who it does it to. — Cory DoctorowWe have internalized the narrative that the way computers work is preordained, and that it is necessary that computers work the way they do currently. We can thank this narrative for the idea that AI is the next step in computing.This puts us in a malaise of fatalism, making it easy to believe that we must accept what we are given — including LLMs and AI — or risk being left behind. We — the people — create technology and computers; we could drive it in a different direction if we wish or abolish it altogether. If people are being left behind, other people are leaving them behind, not technology.It’s easy to see technology as something like the laws of nature — offering us gifts like solar power or antibiotics — but it also shares a great deal with fashion: a succession of trends, driven not just by utility, but significantly by imitation and novelty. Packaged technology — like computers, operating systems, applications — has much much more to do with peers and predecessors in their category and with cultural norms regarding how we work with information than it have to do with logic and physics.Ignore — as Cory Doctrow advises in The Reverse Centaur’s Guide to Life After AI — those who say “there is no alternative” (TINA). IBM said there was no alternative to the mainframe, and DEC proved overwise with the minicomputer and later Apple with the microcomputer; Microsoft said there is no alternative to Windows and Linus Torvalds proved otherwise with Linux.AI fatalism rides along with two other ideas:AI will save the world (e.g. cure cancer).AI will destroy the world (e.g. kill us in a “Terminator-style” scenario).These are really two sides of the same idea: that AI will, sometime in the future, attain awe-inspiring abilities and change the fate or our species. These claims are usually broached in terms familiar to most people but without practical specifics, or are otherwise nonsensical.This serves to distract people from real questions relevant to AI today — whether and how to implement AI, how to handle datacenters, whom to complain to that you have to talk to a machine to get customer service, how to protect your data, how to respond to slop — and have them focus instead on fantasies.This distraction gains much ground thanks to “CEO said” journalism, first christened by Chris Kottke, wherein journals will print nonsense if a CEO said it. Journalists have a moral obligation to challenge the facts and perspectives of their subjects, and especially the executives of influential and well-capitalized companies.We should evaluate AI and any other technology on its merits, without distraction from fatalism, hype and nonsense.3. Humanity: pretend AI personalitiesClippyYou’ll have these little “Max Headroom” characters with bow ties, who you have to talk to. […] Having to deal socially with inane objects that pretend to understand you, but don’t, is much worse than a cocktail party. It’s absolutely unnecessary; it’s a council of despair. — Ted NelsonWe anthropomorphize everything, and technology companies are quick to encourage this: from the original Macintosh’s jaunty mouth, to Microsoft’s Clippy.Large language models are so good at talking that many truly believe them to be conscious or to have personalities. LLMs have neither personhood nor personality: monitoring them to use and respond to first person pronouns is deceptive — more so, say, than Clippy because LLMs are so good at talking.Names and personal pronouns are for intelligent beings with personalities: having people use them for LLMs puts the user in a posture of equality with the machine, which, given the growing power-imbalance between the supercorporations fielding LLMs and people, puts the machine above the human in the power relationship.Conversely, we and our corporations and governments find it just as easy to dehumanize people: sometimes through lurid oppression, sometimes merely through bureaucratic drudgery. It is not fair to expect someone hanging onto their dignity by a thread to talk to a machine as though it has a personality (more so to require them to do) in order to proceed with whatever work, government or customer service task is required of them.The prospectus of the LLM includes a promise to help users manage information: particularly to find the information they need, or to contextualize their work. Such solutions, however, rarely actually organize the underlying information.While people are making some progress, such as with graph databases and markdown files, AI’s insights are typically not stored (nor is the underlying information modified) as durable links/folders/database rows, to shape information for a future date or for other people. While AI can work between silos (e.g. large information repositories like Drive and SharePoint) it creates no workable, standalone connections between them.LLMs promote personality at the expense of durability and interoperability. AI gives users the impression that something conscious is helping them to get organized, while their (and our society’s) information’s chaos deepens.Machines are tools: they should respond predictably to unambiguous inputs. Putting a human persona on a machine does nothing but diminish the real human.4. Information: siren servers and the new enclosureA memorial to 40 people slain while protesting the enclosure of the common land which supported them. | Image by Richard CroftAn economy where advertisers thrive while journalists and artists struggle, reflects the values of a society more interested in deception and manipulation than in truth and beauty .— Jaron LanierIn Who Owns the Future?, philosopher Jaron Lanier laid out his theory of the “siren server” — that modern companies have developed a new business model, which generates a competitive advantage by having more data and thus greater insights to leverage.This is a new form of competitiveness: it is not the same advantage that was afforded, say, to IBM by its huge network of relationships, partnerships and salespeople; or its ability to spend colossal sums on research and development.Siren servers do not compete by innovating (at least not when they’re mature) — they compete by being big. As a result, siren servers are incentivized to get as big as possible, as quickly as possible, leading to business practices directly misaligned with user needs:Free/artificially low pricing to enroll users, who are then monetized by degrading the performance of the service and/or by new fees. (Don’t confuse this tactic for the “free trial” approach; the siren server fees are a surprise.)Barriers to leaving, such as incompatibility (e.g. enterprise information management solutions that cannot talk to each other).Invasive advertising.Some siren server systems felt like progress at the time, but with any kind of hindsight, this is not progress. As Doctrow outlines in Enshittification, would anyone claim, for instance, that:Today’s large, closed social networks would be worse if they allowed some measure of interoperability, e.g. that one could message one’s friends there without an account (as one can with email)?People like to be followed around by advertisers?People feel good about or don’t have a bad taste in their mouth from having rushed onto free/cheap platforms in the 2010s, to find those platforms turned into cattle-pens?It’s arguable that modern LLM companies represent the perfection of the siren server model. They aggregate incomprehensible volumes of data, in order to deliver an informational advantage to their users.As Lanier has also observed, this results in a peculiar and new type of economic displacement: of workers (e.g. translators, writers, designers, etc.) by tools that simulate them.Lanier points to the example of translators, who have been obviated significantly by translation AIs that used their translations as raw material. The fact of simulation is critical: AI doesn’t displace people with a new tool — unlike and regardless of the moral nature, say, of replacing horses with cars or canals with trains — today, thousands of people have been and will be displaced by simulations based on their work.Currently, no legal protections exist, as Doctrow explains in Reverse Centaur. There is much discussion of copyright, but this relates primarily to AI firms’ illegal use of copyright material, i.e. downloading without paying for it. We face a new question: how should we treat the aggregation of people’s material to form systems which then put the same people out of the job?Throughout human history, we have created new rights to respond to new situations: working time, copyright, patents, zoning, etc. Copyright, for instance, became relevant after the printing press made reproducing texts inexpensive. In some cases, like working hours, many unions and managers have come to acceptable settlements. (Though there is still much to discuss.)In other cases, such changes gave way to colossal and irrevocable wealth transfers. Perhaps the most relevant example was the enclosures in Britain. For centuries, poor farmers had the right to graze cattle on the commons — land then considered inferior for farming but still useful for the people to support themselves.As agricultural technology improved, this land became profitable and, over several centuries, landowners enclosed the commons and denied commoners the right to graze. There are still commoners and there is still common land, but this displacement was large enough to cause the exodus from the countryside to the cities which peopled the industrial revolution.Large organizations are launching an enclosure today: they are aggregating information we thought had no value, and giving it a value. We think that we should form a new settlement (for instance Lanier’s “data as labor”) which provides both for the right of individuals and groups to scrape and study information (including “training” AI) and for the people to make something of their newly valuable data.Beyond this, we need to wake up to the fact that anything we create can potentially be used as “training data” and therefore must never again simply create (and share) something without first asking who will use it, whether we approve of that usage, and whether therefore it requires protection.5. AI by force, and as forceAn interface is humane if it is responsive to human needs and considerate of human frailties. — Jef RaskinAll tech companies are fond of making us aware of their new features. Companies are fond also of pushing unwanted new features, such as by taking up screen space previously available for other uses, or making a feature that previously stood alone accessible only via a new one. This has reached its zenith with AI.Appealing to the idea that software should help the user, and should act as a tool, software should not interfere, block, or interpose itself between the user and their work. (This is distinct from “doing precisely what they want, immediately” because software is duty-bound to protect a user from accidentally deleting their writing, for instance.)Software companies can make people aware of new AI (and other) features without violating the contract set out above. Meanwhile, users should have access to simple, conventional data access features: such as searching, filtering, results lists and tables when companies can make (and have previously made) them available.Bosses also frequently insist that employees use AI, and some job applications make AI-use a criteria (rarely for the application itself, ironically). Given the harm and uncertainty wrought by AI, bosses should afford conscientious objectors respect and possibly rights, as we do for people with their views on war, social relationships, the environment, etc.Meanwhile — as part of a broader trend to deny users access to effective customer service (hiding phone numbers/contact information, customer help labyrinths) — companies are now making customer service available only through AI, and are scaling down their human teams. Companies have every right to deploy tools to help (some people prefer AI customer support) but not to remove avenues of communication and accountability, especially in situations where only humans can provide meaningful help.Software should help its users, companies should help their customers and respect their employees — let us not let AI confuse straightforward questions.DemandsTherefore, we demand an end to:The AI bubble.Fatalism, hype, and to “CEO said” journalism.Pretend software personalities, possessed by AI or otherwise.Siren servers — companies that compete only through size and data aggregation.Companies forcing AI on users, to bosses forcing AI on employees, and of AI as a barrier between people and organizations.And, in their place, we demand:Sustainable, broad-based economic growth with broad benefits.Sound, grounded, factual discourse on AI.The choice to use conventional information retrieval interfaces.A new settlement to remunerate people for the use of their newly valuable data.The right to object to AI and to be afforded reasonable protections for doing so.Coda: why are we here?A screenshot from an early file-manager program developed at Xerox PARC. | Image by Damien.bUntold reams of paper, not to mention U.S. Federal money, has gone to waste on the tall tales of artificial intelligence. […] People want control over their computers and their lives. So far, even the supposedly-controllable software is uncontrollable; would you trust today’s developers to create things you can understand even less? — Ted NelsonEstimates vary, but it’s likely that knowledge workers spend around 20% of every workday just looking for information. Generally, computer users complain that:They cannot find the information they need on their computer or in the cloud.Projects get out of hand and become unmanageable, and are often abandoned.Their work, especially in collaboration with others, is hampered by the fact that different file types and information systems don’t work together.Generally, their ideas aren’t shaped like documents and spreadsheets.How did we get here? Ted Nelson theorizes that “it all went wrong at Xerox PARC.” PARC: where in the public imagination the ideas behind modern computing like windows, the mouse pointer, text editing, etc. were developed.At PARC, the computer — a machine capable of creating and associating information in any way — became a machine instead for undertaking minor secretarial tasks like creating and filing paper documents, rather than building ideas. People feel like they need AI because today’s software isn’t up to the task of expressing, organizing and connecting our ideas.Users are looking for better tools to help them get organized because our information systems destroy information; companies hold out AI as the solution, when in fact it is part of the same mistake, and will make users’ problems much much worse.Rather, we need a new approach, that:Lets users own and control their data.Puts up no barriers between information systems (folders on your drive versus database), datatypes (e.g. document versus email) and repositories (SharePoint versus Drive).Allows users to create a growing, adapting web of durable, shareable relationships between their ideas.After the AI bubble bursts — or otherwise when we can look at computers with clarity — let us devote the energy and creativity we need to build software subtle enough to conform to the shape of human thought.After the AI bubble: a manifesto was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
