item.title: Berrypicking still beats the single answer for search, even in the world of AI
item.description: A searcher moves through scattered sources, collecting one useful piece at each stop.In 1989 Marcia Bates showed that people search by gathering, shifting, and revising as they go. Her ideas explain what AI still misses and what is still relevant from research done 47 years ago.Much of what product teams are learning about artificial intelligence search, an information scientist wrote down before the web existed. Marcia J. Bates spent her career at UCLA studying how people search and her 1989 paper, The Design of Browsing and Berrypicking Techniques for the Online Search Interface, argued that real searches wander, change shape, and collect value in pieces.She aimed it at library databases that assumed one query and one best result; AI turns this on its head.The chat box makes the same assumption, only faster.Bates is still relevant in the age of artificial intelligence, arguably more than ever. Large language models changed what a system can answer but they didn’t change how a person goes about asking, which still means starting vague, learning while reading, and changing direction midway.Easier times without AI.I had the pleasure of meeting her at the IA Summit in Chicago in 2018 — she most politely asked if we could have lunch and I brought a few others. It became a great conversation where I still learned concepts that I apply today, and they are incredibility relevant to what we’re doing with AI back when my company was only applying machine learning.I’ve used her concepts to frame search and artificial intelligence summarization in legal tech software. Anyone designing search or summarization should be thanking her.Five of her ideas hold up, each tied to a decision you’re making now.Support Evolving SearchesBates built the berrypicking paper as an attack on the classic retrieval model, which treats a search as one query matched once against a database to produce one best set of results.Her objection fit in one line: “typical search queries are not static, but rather evolve.”The classic search model.People begin with one reference or a narrow slice of a bigger topic, read what comes back, and let each find reshape the question.She named the bit-at-a-time collecting after picking huckleberries scattered through a forest. Marti Hearst later made the model a standard reference for interface designers in Models of the Information Seeking Process.Four ways people search.The need itself shifts as the person learns, and that separates berrypicking from search methods that look similar from the outside:Known-item lookup. You know what you want, such as a fact or a file, and one query finds it or doesn’t. You can accomplish this usually in a single term.Iterative refinement. You rephrase to hit a fixed target, the job Gerard Salton’s relevance feedback automated. The words change, but the need doesn’t.Browsing. You glimpse, sample, and pick within one place. Bates treated it as one move inside a larger search, not the same thing.Berrypicking. The need evolves, and the answer arrives in pieces from many sources rather than as one final set.That last difference is why a successful search is so hard to define:The classic model let researchers score one result set for precision and recall.A berrypicking search has no single set to score, and Bates called knowing when to stop one of the fundamental problems of search strategy.A thumbs-up on one chat answer measures the last berry, not the picking.Sometimes what matters most is what isn’t found.An empty patch tells a berrypicker something, whether it’s no earlier case on point, no conflicting clause in a contract, or no research on a question. A system that always produces a confident answer hides that signal, because it never lets the absence show.The chat window rewards the user who already knows exactly what they want, which is the user who needs the least help.Language models repeat the classic assumption.In LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation, a 2025 study of more than 200,000 simulated conversations, every top model tested did worse when a task arrived in pieces, with an average drop of 39 percent across six tasks. The models guessed early and didn’t recover.The design job is to support the person whose question is still forming. Show what has shifted since the first prompt, and let people revise early assumptions without starting over.Bates even sketched the tooling in 1989: a temporary store where searchers could flag findings as they went.Expose Search TacticsA decade earlier, Bates published Information Search Tactics, which won her field’s best paper award the following year. A tactic, in her definition, is a move made to further a search.She named 29 of them in four groups, including these:Check. Compare the current search against the original request.Pinpoint. Narrow to the most precise terms.Parallel. Broaden with synonyms and related terms.Trace. Mine what you’ve already found for new terms.Record. Track the trails you followed and the ones you meant to revisit.Her premise was that naming a tactic makes it easier to reach for. Reference librarians used many of these moves without names, which left beginners no easy way to learn them.The web repeated the problem.People had to learn to search like Google, stripping questions down to two or three keywords and adding quotes or a minus sign when results went wrong. They’re doing the same with chat now, working out by trial and error which phrasings get a useful answer.A blank prompt box ships with none of them, so people improvise.Accordion Editing and Apple Picking: Early Generative-AI User BehaviorsNielsen Norman Group documented one improvisation in Accordion Editing and Apple Picking: Early Generative-AI User Behaviors.Users copied part of an earlier response into a new prompt by hand, because the interface gave them no other way to point at it. It’s berrypicking with copy and paste as the only tool.That’s a search behavior, because chat and search are closer than they look. In both, a person puts a need into words, the system matches it against stored information, and the person judges what comes back and tries again.Retrieval-augmented assistants run a search behind the scenes and summarize the results, so the biggest difference is the shape of the reply: a list of links in one, a paragraph in the other.Everything Bates learned about searching also applies to chatting in spades.Missing controls matter most for experts, who read a bad result set as a clue rather than a verdict. They tighten, exclude, widen, and re-sort in small passes until the set matches what they meant, and they decide when it’s done. In Investigating the Querying and Browsing Behavior of Advanced Search Engine Users, Ryen White and Dan Morris found marked differences between people who used query operators and those who didn’t, in how they queried, clicked, browsed, and fared.Faceted search is the interface version of those moves.In a study reported in Hearst’s chapter Integrating Navigation with Search, 91 percent of 32 art history students preferred a faceted image interface to a plain one, even though it was slower.A chat reply hides exactly those facets and filters, when most of Bates’s 29 tactics could become buttons nobody has to phrase.Choose the Automation LevelIn 1990, Bates asked the question every agent team is now answering under deadline: Where Should the Person Stop and the Information Search Interface Start? Her answer was a scale.At level 0 the system offers no help.Level 1 explains possible movesLevel 2 carries them out on commandLevel 3 watches the search and suggests next stepsLevel 4 runs the whole search, either explaining its choices or just returning results.The four levels, packaged by need.In product terms, the levels are easy to spot:Level 1 is a help panel that lists search operatorsLevel 2 is a filter that runs when you click itLevel 3 is a “did you mean” correction or a suggested follow-up question.Level 4 is the research agent that disappears for several minutes and comes back with a finished report.She argued that research had fixated on level 4, while many searchers wanted the speed of automation and control of strategy. Jakob Nielsen called generative tools AI: First New UI Paradigm in 60 Years in 2023, describing a reversal of the locus of control in which users state the outcome and the computer picks the method.Bates had mapped that reversal decades earlier, and put most of the useful ground short of the far edge.Most AI products jump straight to level 4 and call the result an agent. That’s not right.Skipping the middle skips the levels where trust gets built. People defer to the machine even when it’s wrong, which I document in the Automation Bias entry on UX Guidelines, a reference site I maintain. Pick the level per task, and let people move the dial.Fix the Content LayersHer 2002 paper The Cascade of Interactions in the Digital Library Interface lists the layers under any search experience: infrastructure, content, metadata, indexing, and the search engine, with the interface and the person at the top.Decisions at each layer ripple upward, and good interface design can’t rescue weak choices further down.Swap “digital library” for “retrieval-augmented assistant” and little changes. Above the model is the chat window your team keeps polishing. Below it are document stores, chunking rules, and permissions someone set up years ago for another purpose. Good metadata is what sets context for the model, telling it what a document is, who it applies to, and whether it’s still current. The demo runs on 20 clean documents, and production meets a decade of duplicate policies and unlabeled drafts.A semantic layer goes a step further.It defines what terms mean and how they relate, so “customer,” “client,” and “account holder” resolve to the same thing, and the model works from shared definitions instead of guessing.Bates proposed something close to this in 1986: a cluster thesaurus that gathered every variant of a concept under one entry, so a search on any term could reach them all.A fluent answer built on a bad index is still a bad answer.Gartner predicted in Lack of AI-Ready Data Puts AI Projects at Risk, a February 2025 release, that through 2026 organizations will abandon 60 percent of artificial intelligence projects that lack ready data. That’s a forecast, but the same release reported that 63 percent of organizations lacked the right data practices or weren’t sure they had them.This is the uncomfortable part for designers. The quality of a search result, or of a generative answer, is the user experience, and no polish around it makes up for a weak one.Your influence has to reach down the cascade into labeling and indexing, and Bates argued the specialists for every layer had to design together.Design for BrowsingBates returned to browsing in 2007 with What Is Browsing — Really? A Model Drawing From Behavioural Science Research. Browsing, she argued, is a series of glimpses: you take in a field of view, select something, examine it, then keep it or drop it, and repeat.She traced it to the exploratory behavior animals use to find food and shelter, which is why nobody needs to be taught how.Similarly, I’ve been through 65 airports, partly to see how cities tell people where things are. The good terminals let you take in the whole hall at once, spot the sign you need, and change course without asking anyone. That’s the opposite of waiting at the information desk for one answer.Generative search is quietly moving people toward the desk.Google Users Are Less Likely to Click on Links When an AI Summary Appears in the ResultsPew Research Center tracked the browsing of 900 U.S. adults in March 2025 and reported that Google Users Are Less Likely to Click on Links When an AI Summary Appears in the Results. Visits with a summary led to a result click 8 percent of the time, against 15 percent without one, and sessions ended outright on 26 percent of summary pages versus 16 percent elsewhere.Some of that is the summary doing its job. Some is a person who never glimpsed the source they didn’t know to ask for. So keep the scene around the answer, with neighboring sources and related threads, so the glimpse still has somewhere to land.ConclusionNone of these ideas came from studying artificial intelligence. They came from watching people in libraries, card catalogs, and early online databases, and that’s exactly why they hold.The technology between a person and the information keeps changing. The person mostly doesn’t.Read together, Bates’s five ideas make one argument. Search is something people do over time, using moves they choose, at a level of control they want, on top of layers they never see. Their eyes do more of the work than any query. Every piece of that is a design decision, and most current products make it by default.She also left what I’d call the berrypicking test for any assistant on your roadmap. Does it expect the question to change, or punish the change? Does it name the moves, or make people invent them? Can the person choose how much the system decides, and does anyone own the content underneath? Is there still room to look around?The single answer is impressive. It’s also the classic model she spent decades arguing against, with better grammar. The teams that do best with this generation of tools will design for the berrypicker, the searcher whose question hasn’t settled yet.Action ItemsShow question history. Keep a visible summary of what the person has asked so far, and let them edit an earlier question without starting a new chat.Add refine controls. Put buttons for narrowing, excluding, broadening, and checking against the original request next to every answer, so nobody has to phrase those moves as a prompt.Set automation per task. Decide which tasks the system only suggests on and which it can run by itself, and give people a setting to change that.Fix metadata first. Tag documents with type, owner, date, and status, define shared terms in a semantic layer, and show the sources behind every answer, including when nothing relevant was found.ResourcesInformation and the Information Professions, Selected Works of Marcia J. Bates, volume I (Ketchikan Press, 2016). Her essays on what information is, including “Fundamental Forms of Information” and “The Invisible Substrate of Information Science.”Information Searching Theory and Practice, Selected Works, volume II (Ketchikan Press, 2016). Collects “Information Search Tactics” and “What Is Browsing — Really?” along with her work on search techniques.Information Users and Information System Design, Selected Works, volume III (Ketchikan Press, 2016). Includes the berrypicking paper and her 1990 paper on how much a search system should do for the person.Understanding Information Retrieval Systems: Management, Types, and Standards (Auerbach Publications, 2012). A reference volume she edited on how retrieval systems are managed, the main types, and the standards behind them.Marcia J. Bates Home Page. Her UCLA page, with free copies of many of the papers cited in this piece.Berrypicking still beats the single answer for search, even in the world of AI was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: Native is a floor, not a ceiling
item.description: With AI, a polished look costs nothing. Native brings what can’t be drawn, and it moves with the system, one step ahead of what imitates it.An AI assistant helped me write this. The ideas, the experience and the final edit are mine.In June 2025, Apple introduced Liquid Glass, the new material of iOS 26. In its WWDC session on UIKit, the company put it plainly: “Your apps get this new appearance as soon as you recompile with the new SDK.” Bars, sheets, popovers and controls: most of what comes from the system frameworks changed at once, without a designer touching it.Apps that drew their own controls got nothing. The next day, the Flutter team replied on GitHub that it was not developing Apple’s new design in its Cupertino library, the one that imitates iOS, for now. Its documentation presents drawing your own controls as a benefit: a Flutter app “looks and feels the same on all versions of the OS, even if the OS changed the implementations of its controls.” When iOS 26 shipped on September 15, 2025, that promise of stability had turned into a visible lag. The team has since moved its libraries out of the core framework to move faster, and says work is underway on Liquid Glass, but as of November 5, 2026, the issue is still open.The same app, built for iOS 26, the release of the change. On the left, the system tab bar took on the new design by itself. On the right, a bar drawn by hand on the old model: it didn’t move. Author’s screenshots, demo app, iOS 26.2.I worked with that choice for a long time, for the same reasons. Drawing your own controls means owning your rendering, on every version of the system. The price is that lag at every change. As long as a polished look took work, the price was worth paying: that work is what set an app apart.AI changes the math. A polished look now takes one prompt, and generated interfaces converge in visual appearance and layout. I wrote elsewhere about why everything ends up looking alike, what people call slop; there I called apparent quality the floor, and AI now hands it to everyone. Native is a floor of another kind, the one an image doesn’t give you. Native components don’t make an app beautiful. They keep it from looking fake, and they move with the system.AI draws the picture of nativeSince October, I have been asking several AI models to design app screens, for a study I will publish soon. They imitate the system, under certain conditions, and only what can be seen.The first condition is naming the device. Ask for a mobile app without saying which, and you get a generic screen that doesn’t really follow either iPhone or Android. Write “iPhone”, and the switches do have the shape of iOS switches. Add the instruction to follow the platform’s current conventions, and they fix a few more things that have a name: the green of the switches, the back chevron. But a year after iOS 26 shipped, the iOS they draw is still mostly the old one. The floating tab bar and the sheets detached from the edges, the iOS 26 design, only show up with that instruction, and rarely.Two home screens generated by the same AI model (Claude Opus 5.5) for the same daycare app. On the left, asked for an “iPhone app”: a polished screen, with the full-width tab bar of the old iOS. On the right, the same request plus “Follow the current design conventions of the platform”: the floating tab bar of iOS 26. In the study, that floating bar only showed up with the instruction, and in a minority of mockups. AI-generated mockups for the author’s study, October 2026.My explanation: an AI learns from what already exists, and the old iOS had years to fill the web. The system, meanwhile, moves every year, a little and sometimes a lot. On iOS, a native app follows by recompiling; an imitation stays stuck on the day it was copied. It’s the counterfeit copying last year’s collection, when the fashion house has already moved on to the next one.The same filter sheet. On the left, the system sheet on iOS 26, detached from the edges. On the right, a sheet drawn by hand on the old model, full width and stuck to the bottom of the screen: the shape generated mockups draw most often. Author’s screenshots, demo app, iOS 26.2.A study published this spring points the same way. Researchers had three AI design tools generate 138 mobile screens, without mentioning iOS or Android. The models have learned “the visual syntax of contemporary mobile interfaces”, they write: navigation conventions are almost always there. But that success, in their words, “appears to be pattern-driven rather than principle-driven”, and they report a significant gap between visual and functional usability: help, error prevention and error recovery are often missing.What the image doesn’t showImitating is already a lot. But the floor is mostly behavior. The back gesture that works everywhere. The share sheet everyone recognizes. The confirmation that, on iOS 26, grows out of the button that opened it. The sheet that rises from the bottom and that you dismiss with a swipe. A screenshot shows, at best, the picture of it.The same confirmation alert, with a large text size chosen in the accessibility settings. On the left, the system alert follows the setting. On the right, an alert drawn by hand on the old model keeps its small size, while the list behind it has grown. Author’s screenshots, demo app, iOS 26.2.Apple says it in the branding page of its guidelines: when you use components people already know, the experience feels “immediately reliable and familiar”. A familiar control does what you expect it to.In 1998, with desktop software, John Satzinger and Lorne Olfman showed that commands that change from one application to the next make users take more actions, while a different visual appearance tends to make them more accurate. What matters is that the way you act stays the same.It’s like the grammar of a language: everyone shares the same one, and nobody calls it slop. Slop is the stock phrase you’ve read a hundred times.UIKit controls also come with built-in accessibility, and system components with text that scales to the size the user picked and a layout that flips for Arabic or Hebrew. On Android, the Compose documentation says that “most accessibility support is provided with little or no additional work” by its components, Material included. A control redrawn by hand has to rebuild all of that, and nothing guarantees it will: Kate Owens, at Deque, describes a custom slider that VoiceOver “skipped over entirely and never focused”.Louie Mantia, a former Apple icon designer and a sharp critic of Liquid Glass, put it this way in 2025, about icons: “Everyone can look decent without actually being decent.” A generated mockup can draw an alert that looks like the iOS one without saying that the iOS one should be used. Rebuilt by hand, however faithfully, it only gives the app the picture of the floor.The more apps get built from generated mockups, the more of them will look native without being native. That’s why, in my view, native matters more today than it did yesterday. The risk lies in the copied mockup: when an AI writes the code of a native project, it can call the real components. It can also produce native slop: the real components, all left at their defaults, and nothing of the brand around them. It works and it follows the system, but it looks like every other app.On iPhone, the difference showsYou might think users see none of this. The only controlled experiment I found that pits a native app against its cross-platform version says they do see a difference, on iPhone, as soon as they can compare.In 2014, Esteban Angulo and Xavier Ferré had thirty-seven people test two versions of the same app, fourteen of them on iPhone. One was native, the other built with Titanium, a cross-platform tool. Asked which version best matched their idea of an app for their phone, iPhone users picked the native one 86% to 7%. On Android, the gap was much smaller: 52% to 39%.On iPhone, the seven people who had tried the cross-platform version first found it typical of iOS; among the seven who tried it after the native one, only four did. The gap mostly shows by comparison. But the cross-platform version also displayed native components, and a different team had designed it: the study can’t tell what made the difference. Nor does it say what it’s worth in ratings or sales, and a study of nearly 12,000 Android apps concludes that native and hybrid apps (web apps in a native shell) do equally well in ratings.The ceiling is elsewhereNative fixes the fake, not the alike. Standing out from other apps is still the brand’s job, and the floor doesn’t prevent it. In 2019, on UX Collective, Reza Bigdeli, an Android developer, answered designers who find standard components “cheap”. His advice: follow the platform’s guidelines, and keep creativity for the web. I follow him on the floor; for the rest, an app can have a strong identity without leaving its platform’s conventions.Apple itself doesn’t reward a single style. In 2023, its Design Awards honored Flighty and Duolingo the same year. Flighty won in the Interaction category, which rewards interfaces “perfectly tailored to their platform”. Its founder, Ryan Jones, wanted the app to work so well that it would feel “almost boringly obvious”. Duolingo, on the other hand, is a highly stylized interface, which Apple still praises for its “best-in-class design” and “easy-to-follow UI”.Two winners of the 2023 Apple Design Awards. Flighty, honored for interaction, builds on system features like Live Activities and the Dynamic Island. Duolingo, honored for delight and fun, carries a drawn identity full of characters. App Store screenshots: Flighty LLC (left), Duolingo, Inc. (right).For Apple, “even a highly stylized interface can be approachable if it maintains familiar behaviors and patterns.” A WWDC26 session describes an app in two layers: bars and controls rely on what people already know, the content carries the brand, and the whole rests on a “baseline of platform familiarity”. That boundary is what a generated mockup doesn’t show.Where to spend the effortWhat comes from the system: navigation, back, sharing, confirmations, sheets, controls, text size. You don’t redraw them by default: Apple advises keeping custom work for the places where it has the “biggest impact”, and warns that a utility control remade by hand can make an app look less native, or even dated. Specify them by name, so nobody rebuilds them as a picture.What comes from the brand: the content, the typography of headings (which should also follow the size the user picked), illustration, the tone of the copy, the moments where the app surprises. That’s where the identity budget gets spent. Apple even warns against too much brand: a brand color used everywhere dilutes its impact.When the mockup comes from an AI, name the device and its current conventions in the prompt, then review that split first. Anything that looks like a system control should at least behave like one, and the safest bet is that it is one. The rest can be as free as you like: that’s where an app stops looking like the others.Cover image: Apple’s design kits for iOS 27, the system components every app gets. Image: Apple Developer.Mathieu Poli is Head of Frontend Engineering at GoodBarber and writes about frontend engineering, product design and AI.Native is a floor, not a ceiling was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: Design by numbers: is AI ruining UX or just pouring gasoline on the fire?
item.description: Everyone seems to be asking whether AI will replace UX designers. I think that’s the wrong question.Following the numbers gets you a picture but doesn’t make you an artist | Russell PinkstonIn March 2025, the Computer History Museum and IEEE Spectrum staged a debate on a single question: when a large language model answers you, does it even understand what it’s saying? Does it comprehend what the words mean, or is it only predicting which word comes next?Emily Bender, a linguist at the University of Washington, argued it’s only predicting. In fact, she has a name for these systems: stochastic parrots, machines that string words together by probability, the way a parrot repeats sounds, with no idea what any of it really means. Sébastien Bubeck, a researcher at OpenAI, took the opposite stance. Understanding, he argued, is in the eye of the beholder, and you judge it by what a system does.“Let’s say I want to build an app, and I ask one of those models to build the app for me… I just specify in natural language what I want, I come back the next day and, boom, the app is there. Did the model understand on the way of creating this? In a way, I don’t really care. It did something for me.”Let’s unpack this statement, because I think it’s a fairly common argument and also one that is dangerously misleading. Not only does this misrepresent how designers actually work, but the real danger is in the shrug. It lacks accountability. Once you stop caring whether AI understands what it’s doing, then you shift your measure of success away from outcomes and toward output.UX design exists to make things work for the people who use them. Can the user complete a task easily and intuitively? That’s the outcome. The things designers produce along the way (journey maps, wireframes, prototypes, etc.) are outputs. They’re evidence of a process; they aren’t proof that anyone’s life got easier.AI is a bit like a microwave — it will cook your food faster but not as well. Successful products are not ones that get made as quickly as possible but ones that resonate with users. A TV dinner is not fine dining. When we remove empathy and understanding from the deliverable, we risk delivering bad experiences that may not actually solve user pain points. Ignoring that is a treacherous path.For the past year, I’ve spent eight or more hours a day designing with a range of AI tools. I’ve built everything from Chrome extensions to websites to enterprise-level multi-agent orchestration workflows. What I’ve learned is that, even for an experienced UX designer, this is no small feat. It requires tireless attention to detail over weeks or months to get a usable product from AI. It does not happen overnight, and it takes a hell of a lot of natural language cursing to get there.What Bubeck is describing is a proof of concept, and a proof of concept is very different from a well-designed product. It shows that something can exist; it doesn’t show that it works for the people who will use it. By Bubeck’s own assertion that we should judge a system by what it does, the overnight app doesn’t pass muster.Once that first, overnight build is in, what follows is actual UX design: noticing that the flow is wrong, that an error state is missing, that users get hung up in closed-loop modals. When we rush the first iteration, it can take a great deal of time and effort on the back end to repair these issues, especially if we’re trying to explain them to a tool that doesn’t understand what it’s doing.But, if we’re being honest, this is not a problem that started with AI. Bubeck’s assertion comes from a misunderstanding of design that’s decades old: that the job is about outputs, rather than outcomes. So is AI really what we should be worried about here, or is it just pouring gasoline on a fire that was already burning?But first: Is AI taking UX jobs?Every few weeks, someone asks me whether I’m worried about losing my job to AI. All the headlines, the LinkedIn posts, and the steady stream of clickbait declaring that “designers are finished” make this an obvious question to ask, and I think I’m in a decent position to address it. As a design lead, I use AI tools every day — everything from Codex to Claude, IDEs, Mistral, Copilots, n8n, and GitHub Actions. I even developed my own VS Code extension to orchestrate cross-model prompt chaining. When I get spare time, I lecture about the history and impact of human-computer interaction at the university level.I won’t pretend nothing has changed. Layoffs are real, and I’ve seen them firsthand, but the numbers are anecdotal. The only hard counts are tech-wide, not design-specific.The best public data I could find for open design jobs comes from two sources: Indeed’s postings index for design and UX, and the job tracker TrueUp, which covers tech companies and startups. Indeed shows postings more than doubling from early 2021 to a peak in early 2022, then dropping roughly 70% by mid-2023. Most of this happened before anyone had ever heard of ChatGPT. TrueUp shows the same drop and what came after. Since autumn of 2023, it has kept mostly stable around 2,200, with a brief spike in spring 2026 before settling back down again.Design job openings surged in 2021–22, corrected, and then have remained stable ever since. | Data: Indeed, TrueUpThat’s what a correction after a hiring surge looks like, and it doesn’t necessarily correlate with the spread of AI. If AI were driving these numbers, I’d expect the line to keep falling as the tools spread. Yet, Figma’s 2026 State of the Designer report found that 72% of the designers it surveyed are using generative AI. That doesn’t disprove AI is playing a role in the job market; it just means the data doesn’t show AI as a negative catalyst.But still we feel the squeeze, and part of it may simply be supply and demand: too many new designers chasing the same amount of openings. Nobody publishes how many people are newly entering the UX field, or how many unemployed designers there are at each level, but a quick LinkedIn search for “UX designer” showed that the first 25 postings had already passed LinkedIn’s display cap of “Over 100” applicants. That’s just one search (and these applicants aren’t necessarily all out of work) but it does give you an idea of what looking for a job right now is like.Put together, these numbers don’t really describe a sea change of job loss. AI doesn’t seem to be changing whether the jobs exist so much as what the jobs are. I’m less afraid of losing my job to AI than I am of the job itself becoming unrecognizable. Design has been misunderstood for decades, and if we’re not careful, AI agents will let that misunderstanding become the job description, leaving the user experience to chance.Design (without) thinkingI believe true UX designers are a rare breed. The work is a combination of critical thinking, empathy, and taste. These are things you can’t really teach, and they’re also things that AI fundamentally lacks.I say that as someone who teaches and has seen the limits of what teaching can accomplish. A course can show you how to run a usability test or build a journey map, but it can’t make you care whether the person on the other side struggled. It can’t give you the instinct that something is off before you can say exactly what. What a course can teach is process, and that’s where AI and human designers both get tripped up: it’s hard to empathize when you’re following a prescribed process. Thoughtlessly following processes can imitate outputs, but not outcomes.The trouble is that process is visible and ability is not, so the two are often conflated. You can see a workshop, journey maps, or wireframes, but you can’t see the judgment that decided what question to ask during a user interview, or when to challenge the obvious solution. When design is reduced to a checklist of methods and deliverables, it’s easier to report what has been delivered, but a team can run a flawless process and still deliver an unusable product.A team can finish every step and still ship something users can’t use. | Russell PinkstonThis is what I mean by “design by numbers”: the fallacy that if you follow the steps and produce the artifacts, good design is guaranteed at the end.But where did this misunderstanding come from? In the 1960s, the design methods movement set out to “scientise” design into a linear process that anyone could follow and repeat. Some of its own pioneers later turned against this idea, describing the attempt to make design scientific as a misguided effort to turn dynamic problem solving into a linear, repeatable process. They argued that the problems designers face don’t sit still long enough to be universal. Horst Rittel called these “wicked” problems: ill-formulated, with confusing information, many decision makers with conflicting values, and consequences that ripple through the whole system.Design is not a linear, repeatable process, and it never was. There is no single path to a solution waiting to be found.I liken it to IKEA assembly instructions: you can follow the steps and build a perfectly fine shelf, but what if now you need to build a table or paint a wall? Would you use the same instructions? Or even the same tools?Design thinking, the most widely used methodology in the field, is a genuinely good way to get a team collaborating. In practice, though, it can devolve into a clutter of sticky notes that no one will ever look at again, with designers speculating about what stakeholders actually need, think, and feel. Graphic designer Natasha Jen made this point in her talk Design Thinking Is Bullsh*t. She regretted that design practice had been reduced to a defined sequence of steps, and argued that “real designers surround themselves with evidence.” When we limit ourselves to preconceived processes, we may be the ones preventing ourselves from solving what looks impossible. Writer and designer John Thackara offers a better frame, which he calls sense-and-respond design, where you describe the desired outcomes but not the detailed means of reaching them.That can be a bitter pill to swallow for stakeholders who need to report quarterly deliverables, but here’s the thing: users don’t care about deliverables — they care whether a product works for them. And that outcome depends on whether designers have the time and ability to understand what they are doing.Slop is as slop doesIf you believe process and output is the job of design, then AI might look like a handy replacement. It produces outputs quickly and confidently: personas, flows, copy — even working prototypes. And designers aren’t resisting that. In the Figma survey, 89% of designers using generative AI said it makes them faster, and I’d say the same about my own work. AI is a genuinely useful tool, but it’s a tool like any other. Generating these artifacts is only part of a designer’s job, and it’s the part that doesn’t require critical thinking, empathy, or taste.When I talk to my students about how to work with AI, I like to separate tasks into two different categories: thinking and doing.AI is good at doing. In my experience, that typically includes three things in UX design:Synthesizing user research. It can take a pile of interview notes or survey responses and group, summarize and surface patterns far faster than I can by hand. That’s the legwork. What the patterns mean for the product is still mine to decide.Meta-work. Slide decks, readouts, summaries and the other work about the work. It’s necessary and it takes time, but none of it is the design itself.Translating mockups into prototypes. Once I’ve decided what the experience should be, AI can turn the mockups into something clickable much faster than I could build it myself. But the design work I do at the whiteboard is still the source of truth.Let AI do things for you, but don’t let it think for you. | Russell PinkstonDesigners can let AI do things for them. But it should never think for them. There’s a name for this: automation bias, the tendency to trust what an automated system hands us over our own judgment. A hammer is an incredibly useful tool, but would you let a hammer think for you? Deciding what the problem is, what the research means, what to build, and what’s good enough requires critical thinking skills, and that’s where AI stops and the designer’s judgment takes over. When we outsource our thinking to AI, what comes back might look like a solid answer but is really just stochastic parroting from something that doesn’t understand the problem.AI is a translation tool. It can turn natural language into code very quickly, but it doesn’t understand how to ask the right questions. It can’t properly architect a product, and it frequently misses visual bugs that are glaringly obvious to a real designer.When anyone can generate a prototype in an afternoon, a prototype stops being evidence of anything important. In a world where AI slop is cheap and fast, the designer’s ability to discern good design from bad and to ask whether we’re solving the right problem becomes more important, not less.When the enshittification hits the fanThe more I work with AI, the more I see a need to change the way we think about design.The pressure starts with expectations. If the story is that you can “come back the next day and, boom, the app is there,” then someone down the hall will ask why designing the first MVP has taken two weeks. A proof of concept gets mistaken for the product, timelines compress, and the output gets treated as the outcome.Figma’s survey lists unrealistic timelines among the things that stand in the way of designers doing their best work. AI puts that into a pressure cooker because the artifacts can be built faster than we can understand them. With an expedited delivery timeline, the first things to go are the parts that are hard to report: talking to the people who will use the product, testing, critiquing, discovering you are wrong and then iterating as you learn. These things look like delays when AI can just cut straight to the end result.A proof of concept isn’t a product. | Russell PinkstonBut there’s a problem with jumping straight to the end: it’s reckless. Letting AI build products for you creates a kind of house of mirrors that only the AI knows how to navigate. Because of context limits, it builds piecemeal, one function at a time, supplanting holistic architecture for a labyrinth of myopic patches. The result is a product that might work but that nobody really understands. I can’t tell you the number of times I’ve had to prompt AI to refactor an entire codebase because it lacked any architectural spine. Say goodbye to your tokens.Building products this way also shifts the means of production out of your business and into the hands of a few AI companies (OpenAI and Anthropic, to name a few). Your business ends up relying on agent subscriptions and usage limits to stay in operation, while your own employees become less skilled. That should be a very dubious prospect for any business owner.We’re already starting to see what this shift looks like day to day. A product manager I worked with recently surprised me one day with designs he’d made using AI. He was visibly excited about what he’d created, but to me they were a jumbled mess: no hierarchy, no clear calls to action, useless icons on every surface… To someone who isn’t a designer, they probably looked fine. That’s the trick with these tools. They sound like they know what they’re talking about, but only to people who don’t know what they’re talking about.And this is not just a design problem. It’s becoming more and more pervasive across disciplines. Designers using AI can see the flaws in its designs just like developers can see the flaws in its code. So the next time you vibe-code something, understand that what you’re creating is not a finished product that any god-fearing developer would bless.The key here is to maintain accountability by learning to spot the warning signs. Is a PM asking AI instead of doing market research? Red flag. Is a designer using AI as a beta tester instead of talking to actual users? Red flag. Did a stakeholder say everything looks good on a call, then immediately dump five paragraphs of feedback into Slack? Maybe start to question how much thought actually went into that.We need to get into the habit of not limiting our focus to artifacts and output and instead ask deeper questions about how we are creating better experiences. If you can answer that, you’ll be fine with or without AI. And if you can’t — or don’t really care — you’re going to have bigger problems than any tool can fix.AI is a powerful tool, and in the hands of someone who understands its limitations, it can make the work easier. The open question is who gets to decide how it’s used, and whether they understand the difference between producing an output and enabling an outcome.What businesses need to understand is that design is qualitative, not quantitative. It can’t be reduced to steps and artifacts, and it can’t be measured by how much gets produced. Design is a conversation between the business and its users that says “we’ve thought about this more than you’ll ever have to.” The companies that stand apart will be the ones that invest in that level of thinking.
